title: CDI Listening Test 58
description: A full Listening test from the CDI practice materials, with the original recording. 4 parts, 40 questions.

parts.title: Part 1

groups.answerRule: Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
groups.template:
Theatre booking
Example Booking for: Pirates
- Date: 8th December (afternoon)
- Name: Fenella [[1]]
- Contact number: 07796 892326
Booking details:
- Type of booking: [[2]] with discount
- Tickets: 3 adults at £ [[3]] each
- Children under 16 at £ [[4]] each
- Requires seats on the [[5]] row of the circle
- One person uses a [[6]]
- Need to have good access to the [[7]]
- Will collect the tickets from the [[8]]
Meals:
- Several people are [[9]]
- Food: [[10]] (cheese and tomato)

questions.explanation: "It's Fenella Bittens. B-I-double-T-E-N-S." — the surname is spelled out.
She books 20 tickets: "So that's a group booking." "Does that mean I get a discount?" "Yes."
"You get a discount of 10% on those tickets, which makes it 23 pounds per person" (the 3 adult tickets).
For the under-16s: "instead of 15 pounds per person, that'll be 12 pounds 50."
She turns down the middle row: "I think we'd need to be right at the back, actually."
"Because we have one child who's a wheelchair user."
"The main thing is we want to be able to get to the lift easily."
Parking is difficult, so: "we've now got an arrangement that you can pick up tickets in the library."
"We've got a few children in the group who are vegetarian."
Pasta isn't available: "we do have pizzas though." "Let's go for those for all of us — cheese and tomato."

parts.title: Part 2

groups.instructions: Which choir does each of the following statements apply to? Choose the correct letter, A, B or C, for each statement.
groups.title: Choirs

questions.text: They specialise in a particular type of music.
questions.explanation: Specialise in a particular type of music — "If you're after a more classical feel, the Caroline Singers tend to focus on madrigals." Blackvale and Mitchelstown both have varied repertoires.

questions.text: They organise social events.
questions.explanation: Organise social events — Mitchelstown "arrange group visits to see operas and attend music festivals. So it can be a great way to make friends."

questions.text: They have recently won a competition.
questions.explanation: Recently won a competition — "Blackvale are the current holders of the Male Voice Choir Award, presented to them just last month." Mitchelstown are only hoping to reach a final.

questions.text: They have recently recorded their first CD.
questions.explanation: Recently recorded their first CD — "Mitchelstown has just joined Blackvale and the Caroline Singers as recording artists for their first CD."

questions.text: They participate in charity events.
questions.explanation: Participate in charity events — "Blackvale donates a percentage of its profits to certain local charities."

questions.text: Elizabeth Arnold thinks people join a choir at work because it gives them a chance to
questions.explanation: Networking is the distractor: "while the thought of networking opportunities might be at the back of some people's mind, it's having the opportunity to switch off and focus on something completely different that they're after" — a break from work.

questions.text: How does a company benefit from setting up a choir?

options.text: less sick leave taken by employees

questions.explanation: "It can help to create a healthier working atmosphere. For example, people who previously didn't get on can find they have something in common" — improved relationships between co-workers.

questions.text: How many members does the John White choir have?
questions.explanation: "They started off four years ago with just five people. That's now risen to 19" — 12 is the average attendance, not the membership.

questions.text: When do the choir have their rehearsals?
questions.explanation: "They found the middle of the day works best" — early morning and late afternoon are both problematic.

questions.text: How does the company support the choir?
questions.explanation: Members themselves pay for refreshments and shirts, but "the company organizes regular sessions with a professional vocal coach free of charge" — paying for singing classes.

▶ 7:07[Narrator] Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen. And for our regular spot on things to do in town, here's our reporter Samuel Cooper.
▶ 7:18It's been fun to write about joining some of our local choirs. Thank you.
▶ 7:24Well, feeling a bit apprehensive about my ability to sing in tune, I recently headed off for rehearsals at the town's three biggest choirs.
▶ 7:34Mitchellstown choir, the Black Bell Male Voice Choir, and the Caroline Singers. I received a very warm welcome at all three choirs.
▶ 7:45They are always on the lookout for new and enthusiastic singers. Now, obviously deciding which choir to join will depend to some extent on your taste in music.

▶ 8:11That's unaccompanied singing without any instruments.
▶ 8:14If you want to meet people who share an interest in music, Mitchellstown Choir is a good place to start. Apart from their own performances, they also arrange group visits to see operas and attend music festivals.

▶ 9:44You may feel unable to join a choir because you're worried you'd struggle to find the time to attend rehearsals because of work or family commitments. Well, there is a solution to that.

▶ 12:02So if you'd like more information about the choirs.

parts.title: Part 3

questions.text: Mike suggests they use the word area to mean
questions.explanation: "It's probably best to use it for place, in the sense of province or whatever" — a geographical location.

questions.text: According to Eva, most people believe that culture

options.text: refers to long-established events and places.
includes modern forms of art and entertainment.
is becoming less linked to particular regions.

questions.explanation: "That would be confirming these old-fashioned ideas that culture has to be something at least 100 years old." "But that is what most people think."

questions.text: Why should they carry out about 200 surveys?

options.text: to provide information about a range of events
to be able to meet the deadline

questions.explanation: "Our tutor said we should have at least 200. Otherwise the information won't actually mean that much" — to get valid results.

questions.text: Which groups of people do they decide to interview?
questions.explanation: "We should just go for the tourists — but from overseas as well as national" — international and domestic tourists.

questions.text: Mike expresses concern at having to ask about

options.text: the amount of money a person has spent.

questions.explanation: "There's one thing that worries me though... the idea of asking people how old they are?" — a person's age.

questions.text: Which form will their results be presented in?
questions.explanation: "Most people find pie charts visually stimulating." "Pie chart sounds good."

groups.instructions: Which tourist attraction will be highlighted in each of the following countries? Choose FOUR answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–G, for each country.
groups.title: Tourist Attractions

questions.text: Mexico
questions.explanation: Mexico — "Mexico celebrates the fact that it produces a huge number of varieties of chillies, and people flock to this special event to taste dishes using them" (C: food festival). Museums are the distractor.

questions.text: Greece
questions.explanation: Greece — "I think we should go for the ruins in this case. The temples and theatres and so on, rather than the food" (A: ancient buildings).

questions.text: Britain
questions.explanation: Britain — "instead of focusing on the countryside and parks, I'd like to find out more about why people go to see plays and musicals" (F: theatre performances).

questions.text: India
questions.explanation: India — "instead of concentrating on the temples or the game parks, we could mention all the different folk dances" (G: traditional dances).

▶ 17:58[Narrator] That is the end of part three. You now have half a minute. Listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
▶ 18:07I'm a past student of this university, and I'm joining some others on this career day to tell you about my job, as it may be something you've never thought of doing. I'm a patent attorney.
▶ 18:21Some of you probably know what that is, but for those of you that don't, I'll explain.
▶ 18:27If someone has a new idea or invention, they can ask for a patent. It gives the owner the right to stop other people from using that invention.
▶ 18:37A patent is granted by the government to inventors or more usually these days to a company . It is for a certain time period, usually a maximum of 20 years.
▶ 18:50So during that period, that idea or invention cannot be claimed to have been invented by someone else. The likelihood of getting a patent is dependent on whether the invention is original or not.
▶ 19:04This is the crucial factor. It will be looked at by a patent examiner, and my job is to convince the examiner that the invention is not just an adjustment to something which already exists.
▶ 19:18In order to get the patent, we need to produce a full description of the invention . It's really important to get the details right.
▶ 19:27Most of you are scientists and the basic requirement of the job is a solid academic background. Often people have studied chemistry or alternatively engineering .
▶ 19:40Because of the nature of the work, this is a crucial starting point. You need to be able to understand how the inventions have come about. On top of that, employers are looking for particular kinds of people.
▶ 19:54They want employees who have excellent communication skills . So you can talk to inventors in terms that they can understand and also ask the right questions.
▶ 20:05These aren't necessarily skills you're taught at university.
▶ 20:10This is an international business as are most nowadays, and it's very convenient to be able to read documents without having to call for translations.
▶ 20:21So if you can understand a foreign language , that's a great asset. You might think it sounds a bit boring from what I've said, but it really isn't. There are lots of advantages to the job.
▶ 20:34It's extremely interesting for a start. For example, I feel I use a range of expertise. I'm not just a scientist, not just a lawyer, but a mixture of the two.
▶ 20:48Although it takes quite a long time to qualify as a patent attorney, anything from four to six years, after that, you can earn a high salary which compares very well with other similar professions.
▶ 21:02There are some disadvantages, of course. It can be rather lonely as you tend to sit in front of a computer for most of the day. Even if you have colleagues, you will all be working separately.
▶ 21:15And there isn't very much flexibility with location. Almost all vacancies for trainees are city-based.
▶ 21:24So if that doesn't appeal to you, you might want to think again. You do get to travel a bit to meetings with clients. And there are also visits to court.
▶ 21:35So what kind of organization might you end up working in? Well, many people work in industrial companies . The big ones have their own patent departments.
▶ 21:48The kind of product you might work with there will range from food to heavy equipment. From biotechnology to the car industry.
▶ 21:58Basically any organization where significant time and money is put into research and development to get ahead of the market. There are also many private practices.
▶ 22:10And some of these will have areas of special interest. Finally, it's possible to get a job in various government offices .
▶ 22:20In those departments, you'll probably be looking at applications for patents and making decisions about them. I really love my job, so I hope I've persuaded a few of you that it's worth thinking about.
▶ 22:34If anyone wants to come and ask questions, I'm happy to answer them.
